summary: This informational memo describes the framework of the Next Steps in Signaling working group for protocols that signal information about a data flow along its path through the network. The NSIS suite is meant to support applications that install or change state in network nodes.

plainLanguage.summary: Imagine sending a note along a road that tells each stop how to treat your packages. This document describes the overall plan for such signalling.

subtitle: The two-layer architecture for signaling along a data flow's path, from QoS reservations to firewall control.

tldr.problem: Signaling that installs or reads per-flow state in the network, as RSVP does for QoS, needed to work in more places and for more purposes than just reservations.
tldr.mechanism: NSIS splits signaling into a generic transport layer (NTLP) that moves messages between adjacent nodes and separate signaling layers (NSLPs) for each application, such as QoS or middlebox control.
tldr.outcome: The framework explains how the layers, addressing, identifiers, routing changes, mobility, NATs and tunnels fit together. It leaves detailed protocol design to later documents.

today: RFC 4080 is an Informational framework published in June 2005, and the unit metadata lists no obsoleting or updating RFC. It describes the architecture and leaves detailed protocol design to separate documents.

sections.title: The Signaling Problem and Scope
sections.content:
The Next Steps in Signaling (NSIS) working group considers protocols for signaling information about a data flow along its path. The path is assumed to be set already by routing; NSIS does not signal to set up routes. Only the path-coupled case and unicast flows are considered at first.

The problem resembles the one RSVP addresses, with two generalizations. Parts of the NSIS suite should be usable in different parts of the Internet without full end-to-end deployment, and signaling should serve more purposes than QoS. The mechanism is a split into a generic lower layer and an upper layer specific to each signaling application. The work covers the generic protocol and, initially, upper layers for QoS and middlebox signaling. Requirements come from other documents, including RFC 3726 and the threats analysis in RFC 4081, which this framework does not replace.
sections.plainLanguage: The old system could only tell stops along the road how much room to save for you. The new plan lets the same road notes do many jobs, like opening a gate or reading a counter.

sections.title: Signaling Concepts
sections.content:
State related to a data flow is installed on NSIS Entities (NEs) along the flow's path; not every node needs an NE. Two NEs that communicate directly are in a peer relationship, which need not equal one IP hop. The memo calls the state a signaling message installs, changes, refreshes or reads network control state.

In path-coupled signaling the messages are routed only through NEs on the data path. In path-decoupled signaling they go to nodes that are off the data path but aware of it; the initial goal of NSIS is the path-coupled case. Signaling can run end-to-end, end-to-edge or edge-to-edge, and a signaling proxy can act for hosts that are not NSIS-aware.

A flow is a unidirectional sequence of packets along one path, defined by a classifier. A session is an application-layer concept for an exchange that needs network state. Unlike RSVP, a session can map to several flows over its life, for example in a make-before-break handover.
sections.plainLanguage: Notes go from one helper along the road to the next, and the helpers keep a small memory about your trip. Your whole trip is the session, and a trip can change roads without being a new trip.

sections.title: The Two-Layer Model
sections.content:
The suite has two layers. The NSIS Transport Layer Protocol (NTLP) moves signaling messages and is independent of any signaling application. Each NSIS Signaling Layer Protocol (NSLP) holds message formats and sequences for one signaling application. The NTLP covers everything between the NSLP and IP.

The working assumption is that the NTLP is hop-by-hop: it only gets a message to the next NE using knowledge of its direct peers. Larger scope, including end-to-end delivery, is built from these peer hops and handled by NSLPs. An NSLP that needs to message a distant node should use another transport, and the memo suggests UDP or DCCP.

Because different NSLPs run on different nodes, an intermediate node can ignore messages it has no NSLP for. This can use a protocol number or router alert option value at the IP layer, or the NTLP can pass the message back unchanged. On state, the NTLP provides uniform message delivery and does not know the application's timers. Soft-state refresh is the NSLP's business, and the NTLP can only give advisory up/down notifications about peers.

Keeping the NTLP to peer scope means that any options or variants in its design only affect direct peers rather than potentially the whole Internet.
sections.plainLanguage: One helper layer passes notes only to the next neighbour. Another layer, which differs per job, understands what the note says. Helpers who do not know that job just pass the note along.

sections.title: What the Transport Layer Does
sections.content:
A message to the next peer can be addressed in two ways. With peer-peer addressing it goes to a neighboring NE closer to the destination. With end-to-end addressing it goes to the flow's destination and an NE on the way intercepts it. The memo does not choose one: finding the next downstream peer usually needs end-to-end addressing, and reverse routing always needs peer-peer.

Transport functions placed in the NTLP include optional bundling of small messages, fragmentation for large messages, optional reliable delivery for state-changing messages (chosen by the NSLP per message), and congestion avoidance so signaling does not overload the network. The lower boundary is the IP layer. Upward, the NTLP offers Send Message and Receive Message, plus application registration, configuration, errors and feedback such as route change indications.

Three identifiers appear at its interfaces. The flow identifier can draw on source and destination addresses, protocol and ports, flow label, the IPsec SPI and the DSCP/TOS field, so signaling is treated like the data by NATs and policy-based forwarding. The session identifier lets signaling follow a session across flow changes; it should be globally unique, for which a large random number is suggested. A signaling application identifier demultiplexes messages to the right NSLP. The only security service assumed in the NTLP is channel security, and the memo says it is an open question what protection is required.
sections.plainLanguage: A note can be handed to the next neighbour by name, or sent toward the final stop and caught on the way. Each note has a label for your trip, your current road, and which job it is for.

sections.title: Routing, Mobility, NATs and Tunnels
sections.content:
Signaling that is addressed like the data may still take a different path because of load sharing, policy-based forwarding or router alert options. Route changes need three things: detection, installing state on the new path, and removing it from the old one. The memo lists seven detection methods, from watching the local forwarding table to sending a probe packet, and says methods based on signaling messages become less effective as refresh rates fall. With soft state, old state vanishes when refreshes stop, but faster teardown may be needed.

Mobility and multihoming generalize route changes. Signaling uses the outer IP headers, so streams to different addresses count as different flows, and the session identifier correlates them. The node where the flows meet is the crossover router. A NAT that is not NSIS-aware leaves addresses in payloads uncorrected, so the NTLP carries flow identification openly enough for an NSIS-aware NAT to rewrite it. For tunnels, the end-to-end signaling is carried through with the data, and signaling for the tunnel itself treats the tunnel as a new flow, recursively.
sections.plainLanguage: Roads change, travellers move and gates rewrite addresses. The notes need a trip label so the helpers can tell that a changed route is still the same trip, and they need to clean up the old stops.

sections.title: Signaling Applications: QoS and More
sections.content:
For QoS signaling the memo defines three roles: the QoS NSIS Initiator (QNI) makes the resource request, the QoS NSIS Responder (QNR) is the endpoint, and a QoS NSIS Forwarder (QNF) passes signaling between them. They work with a Resource Management Function (RMF) that allocates the network resources. A possible set of messages is Request, Modify, Release, Accept/Reject, Notify and Refresh. A refresh only extends a reservation's life.

When routes change, a reservation exists on the old path until the next control message reaches the new one. RSVP's local repair is one remedy; pre-installing backup state is another. Other signaling applications include setting flow-related state in middleboxes such as firewalls and NATs, network monitoring and testing, and tunnel endpoint discovery.
sections.plainLanguage: For reserving road space, one person asks, the stops in between pass it on, and the far end answers. A separate manager decides how much space really exists.
